title: Count Bit Runs With an Exact Sum
statement:
You get an array bits where every value is 0 or 1, and an integer goal. Count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose values add up to exactly goal.

Subarrays at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same values.

examples.why: Every answer contains both 1s. It may start at index 0 or 1 and end at index 3 or 4: 2 × 2 = 4.
Three subarrays hold only the first 1 ([1], [1,0], [1,0,0]) and three hold only the last. The zeros multiply the count.
Every one of the 6 subarrays sums to 0. A goal of 0 is where many window tricks break.

hints: With prefix sums, a subarray sums to goal when P[j] − P[i] = goal. How can a hash map count matching starts for each end?
Alternatively: the number of subarrays with sum exactly goal is (sum at most goal) − (sum at most goal − 1). Counting "at most" is a normal sliding window.
For "at most g": grow the right end, shrink the left while the window sum exceeds g, and add the window length right − left + 1 for every right end. Return 0 when g < 0.

explain.intuition:
Exact-sum windows are awkward to slide: with zeros around, many left ends work for the same right end, and the window cannot tell when to stop shrinking. "At most" windows are easy. For each right end, the valid left ends form one unbroken range, and the window length counts them all at once.

Then subtract: subarrays with sum exactly goal = those with sum at most goal minus those with sum at most goal − 1. The same answer comes from prefix sums and a hash map that counts how often each prefix value has appeared, which also works when values can be negative.
steps: In atMost, move right across the array, adding bits[right] to sum.
While sum > g, subtract bits[left] and move left right.
pitfalls: Sliding a single window for the exact sum. It undercounts as soon as zeros sit at the left edge.
Calling atMost(-1) without a guard. The inner loop moves left past right and the count goes wrong for goal = 0.
In the hash-map version, forgetting to seed the map with prefix 0 seen once, which drops subarrays that start at index 0.

complexity.space: O(1) for the window, O(n) for the hash map

solutions.title: Check every subarray
solutions.idea: Fix a start, extend the end, keep a running sum and count the hits.

solutions.title: Prefix sums with a hash map
solutions.idea: For each end, the number of good starts is how many earlier prefixes equal the current prefix minus goal.

solutions.title: At most goal minus at most goal − 1
solutions.idea: Two plain sliding windows. Each counts subarrays with sum at most some bound; their difference is the exact count.

followups: Count subarrays with exactly k odd numbers in an array of arbitrary integers. How does it map onto this problem?
The values can now be any non-negative integers. Which of the three solutions still work?
